1.title: The Five-Ticket Promise
1.story:
Verified Fan Identity (VFI) promises to reduce automated ticket buying by limiting purchases to five tickets per verified person, per event.

Major promoters are interested. Fans hope for fairer access, although some are concerned about identity requirements.

Your company can enter this market, but the technology is still developing.
1.question: How will you approach VFI?

options.title: A. Build internally
options.outcome: Your company invests €2.8M in its own system. Recruitment begins, creating skilled employment opportunities. Fans will wait longer for verified ticketing, and financial reserves fall to €3.2M.

private.ceo: The investment may support long-term growth, but financial reserves are tighter.
private.cfo: Only €3.2M remains available for unexpected costs and employment obligations.
private.cto: Your team controls the design and bears responsibility for its reliability.
private.marketing: Fans must wait for the promised benefits.
private.legal: Your company directly controls data practices and implementation decisions.
private.employee: Recruitment opportunities increase, alongside delivery pressure.
private.sustainability: Infrastructure choices remain under company control.
private.relations: Northstar may not wait for your development timetable.

options.title: B. License a provider
options.outcome: Your company signs a supplier agreement. Fans may benefit from verified ticketing sooner. Some technical work moves outside the company, while customer support prepares for new verification disputes. Cash remaining: €5.4M.

private.ceo: Faster delivery may protect major contracts, with recurring obligations.
private.cfo: Recurring fees may eventually compete with staffing and service budgets.
private.cto: Customers will depend on a system your engineers cannot fully modify.
private.marketing: Earlier availability could improve access if verification works well.
private.legal: Responsibility for identity disputes must be clarified with the supplier.
private.employee: Technical work shifts externally; support employees face new demands.
private.sustainability: Supplier practices will influence energy use and accessibility.
private.relations: Northstar's preferred timetable appears achievable.

options.title: C. Hybrid development
options.outcome: Your company combines external verification with internal development. Existing employees will receive new responsibilities and training. The approach creates employment opportunities and integration demands. Cash remaining: €4.4M.

private.ceo: The board expects progress from both internal and external teams.
private.cfo: Development and supplier costs will both require monitoring.
private.cto: Your engineers can shape the experience but depend on external verification.
private.marketing: Customer experience can be adapted, although delivery remains uncertain.
private.legal: Shared responsibilities require clear contractual and technical boundaries.
private.employee: Training opportunities increase, but so does workload.
private.sustainability: Both supplier and internal practices will affect sustainability.
private.relations: Northstar's timetable remains uncertain.

options.title: D. Wait and observe
options.outcome: Your company continues conventional ticketing. Customers avoid new identity requirements, but automated purchasing remains a problem. Employees retain existing responsibilities, while some promoters consider alternative suppliers. Cash remaining: €5.85M.

private.ceo: Preserved cash protects flexibility, but future contracts remain uncertain.
private.cfo: Reserves remain strong, although future revenue is uncertain.
private.cto: Existing systems remain reliable, while the scalping problem continues.
private.marketing: Customers avoid verification barriers but remain exposed to scalpers.
private.legal: Current data practices continue, with fewer new obligations.
private.employee: Existing jobs remain stable for now, with fewer new opportunities.
private.sustainability: No major infrastructure expansion occurs; ticket access remains unchanged.
private.relations: Northstar may seek another provider, affecting future employment and revenue.

info.ceo: The board wants growth within three years. Directors also worry that losing major clients could eventually threaten the company's 120 jobs.
info.cfo: Licensing costs €900K annually after launch, compared with €450K for building and €650K for hybrid. Financial pressure could eventually force staffing reductions or higher service fees.
info.cto: Internal development requires recruiting specialists. External systems are faster, but your engineers cannot yet verify how reliably they prevent duplicate identities.
info.marketing: Fans strongly support anti-scalping measures, but some worry about submitting identity documents. A complicated process could exclude customers who already struggle with digital services.
info.legal: Identity verification is possible under EU law, but each design requires a lawful basis and appropriate safeguards. Supplier contracts currently leave some responsibilities unclear.
info.employee: Building could create skilled jobs. Licensing may shift technical work to suppliers, while verification disputes could increase pressure on customer support staff.
info.sustainability: Verification requires additional computing resources. Some customers lack conventional identity documents, potentially limiting access to events even when tickets are available.
info.relations: Northstar Live, representing 18% of company revenue, wants VFI within twelve months. Several smaller venues worry about the cost of helping customers who cannot verify themselves.

2.title: The Pilot Problem
2.story:
Early VFI trials show promising results against automated purchasing. They also reveal problems: customers struggling with verification, failed transactions, and support teams overwhelmed during major ticket releases.

Your company has limited resources to prepare its technology and services.
2.question: Where should you concentrate your efforts?

options.title: A. Stress testing
options.outcome: Your engineers identify and resolve several capacity problems. Major sales are better protected against technical failure, but customers experiencing verification difficulties still have limited support.

private.ceo: Reliability improves, supporting client confidence.
private.cfo: Testing costs €300K and may prevent expensive failures.
private.cto: Technical reliability improves.
private.marketing: Customer experience remains a potential weakness.
private.legal: Technical testing creates useful evidence of precautions.
private.employee: Engineers face intensive testing demands.
private.sustainability: Infrastructure efficiency becomes better understood.
private.relations: Promoters gain evidence of reliability.

options.title: B. Customer testing
options.outcome: Your team improves registration and support procedures. More customers can complete transactions successfully, although peak-demand reliability remains less thoroughly tested.

private.ceo: More customers can use the service successfully.
private.cfo: Support improvements cost €250K.
private.cto: Customer-facing weaknesses receive attention.
private.marketing: Registration becomes easier for more customers.
private.legal: Customer rights and dispute procedures improve.
private.employee: Support staff receive greater attention and training.
private.sustainability: Accessibility barriers are reduced.
private.relations: Artists gain reassurance about customer access.

options.title: C. Accelerate delivery
options.outcome: The project moves closer to launch. Promoters welcome the progress, but employees report increased overtime and several customer-facing problems remain unresolved.

private.ceo: Delivery advances, but operational pressure grows.
private.cfo: Spending is lower today, with unresolved future costs.
private.cto: Less time remains to resolve known technical problems.
private.marketing: Early launch could attract attention, including complaints.
private.legal: Known customer-facing weaknesses remain unresolved.
private.employee: Overtime and workload pressure increase.
private.sustainability: Accessibility and efficiency remain less thoroughly examined.
private.relations: Early availability may help secure contracts.

options.title: D. Independent assessment
options.outcome: External specialists identify technical, accessibility and operational weaknesses. The findings provide useful evidence, but addressing them will require additional work.

private.ceo: Independent findings may require changes to the timetable.
private.cfo: Review costs €350K, with remediation potentially required.
private.cto: Independent findings provide a prioritized technical assessment.
private.marketing: Findings may strengthen the credibility of future claims.
private.legal: The review documents obligations requiring follow-up.
private.employee: Employees may face additional remediation work.
private.sustainability: The review identifies social and environmental impacts.
private.relations: Clients may appreciate the review or worry about delays.

info.ceo: The board wants progress, but a failed launch could damage relationships with clients who depend on reliable ticket sales for their livelihoods.
info.cfo: Delays increase costs. However, a major ticketing failure could require refunds and compensation that reduce funds available for wages and operations.
info.cto: Stress tests have revealed possible bottlenecks during simultaneous purchases. You cannot guarantee these will occur in normal operations.
info.marketing: Early trials show some fans abandoning purchases when asked to upload identity documents. Others appreciate the reduction in automated buying.
info.legal: Customers must have meaningful ways to exercise their rights and challenge verification errors. The company's procedures remain incomplete.
info.employee: Support staff report increasing overtime during trial periods. Several employees have requested additional training and clearer escalation procedures.
info.sustainability: Verification failures may disproportionately affect customers with limited digital access or documentation. Infrastructure testing could also identify unnecessary energy consumption.
info.relations: Promoters fear cancellations and entry delays. Several artists are concerned that genuine fans may be excluded by verification failures.

3.title: Opening Night
3.story:
Northstar Live is preparing a major European tour and inviting ticketing providers to bid.

The contract could help your company recover from the economic slowdown and support employment. Northstar expects reliable sales, fair access and effective customer support.

An ambitious proposal could bring significant revenue, but failures would affect thousands of fans and people whose livelihoods depend on the tour.
3.question: What will you offer?

options.title: A. Full VFI rollout
options.outcome: Northstar awards your company the full tour contract. Your verified ticketing system meets the required readiness threshold, and implementation begins.

private.ceo: Growth potential rises, alongside responsibility for major delivery failures.
private.cfo: Revenue potential rises, but so does compensation exposure.
private.cto: Thousands of customers may depend on your system's readiness.
private.marketing: Successful delivery could improve access for many fans.
private.legal: Contractual and customer obligations increase substantially.
private.employee: Staffing demands increase, potentially protecting jobs while intensifying workload.
private.sustainability: Accessibility arrangements become critical at scale.
private.relations: A successful tour could strengthen your largest client relationship.

options.title: B. Limited VFI pilot
options.outcome: Northstar awards your company a limited pilot. Your verification system is ready for selected events, with expansion dependent on performance.

private.ceo: A smaller commitment may provide evidence for expansion.
private.cfo: Financial exposure is more limited.
private.cto: Problems can be identified in a smaller deployment.
private.marketing: Customer experience can be evaluated before expansion.
private.legal: Obligations are limited to the pilot scope.
private.employee: Additional work is concentrated around selected events.
private.sustainability: Impacts can be assessed with fewer attendees.
private.relations: Northstar may expand the partnership after the pilot.

options.title: C. Conventional ticketing
options.detail: Existing platform with additional fraud controls
options.outcome: Northstar selects your conventional ticketing service. The company will deliver established ticketing with enhanced fraud monitoring.

private.ceo: The company relies on proven services during uncertainty.
private.cfo: Implementation costs remain manageable.
private.cto: Existing infrastructure remains central.
private.marketing: Fans avoid verification barriers but remain exposed to scalping.
private.legal: Existing service obligations remain.
private.employee: Existing teams continue familiar operations.
private.sustainability: Existing access arrangements continue.
private.relations: Northstar may prefer another provider for VFI events.

options.title: D. Decline
options.detail: Focus on current clients and operations
options.outcome: Your company does not submit a bid. Existing operations continue.

private.ceo: Future growth and employment security remain concerns.
private.cfo: Cash is preserved, with no new contract revenue.
private.cto: No additional technical commitments arise.
private.marketing: The company has less influence over the tour's ticketing experience.
private.legal: No new Northstar liabilities arise.
private.employee: No additional workload, but fewer opportunities for employment growth.
private.sustainability: No new deployment impacts arise.
private.relations: Northstar will seek another supplier for this tour.

info.ceo: Northstar's contract could protect jobs during the downturn. A failed delivery could damage the company's ability to retain other clients.
info.cfo: The full contract offers substantial revenue, but service failures could trigger compensation payments. Existing reserves may be insufficient for an expensive recovery.
info.cto: Your team's readiness depends on earlier testing. Promising demonstrations do not guarantee reliable performance during a major public launch.
info.marketing: Northstar's audience includes customers with limited experience of digital verification. Failed registrations could mean losing access to tickets they expected to purchase.
info.legal: Northstar's proposed contract includes service-level obligations. Customer refunds, disputes and accessibility complaints may create additional responsibilities.
info.employee: A full rollout requires extended customer support coverage. Staff are concerned about overtime, and some fear that failures will lead to disciplinary action.
info.sustainability: Northstar expects accessible ticket purchasing and entry. Customers unable to complete verification may need alternative arrangements.
info.relations: Northstar has other suppliers available. Artists want to reduce scalping but are concerned about fans being excluded or stranded at venue entrances.

proposals: Your company proposes verified ticketing across the tour. Thousands of fans could benefit from reduced scalping, but successful delivery requires reliable verification and effective customer support.

4.title: More Than a Ticket
4.story:
Ticket sales are recovering. Promoters want services that encourage repeat purchases and make events more convenient.

Your product team proposes expanding customer accounts with loyalty rewards, flexible reservations and easier ticket transfers.

These services could generate new revenue and help fans access events, but they require investment and ongoing support.
4.question: Which service will you prioritize?

info.ceo: The board wants new revenue sources. Directors disagree about whether customer retention or market expansion should come first.
info.cfo: Reservations delay incoming cash and leave some tickets temporarily unavailable. Rewards create future redemption obligations that must be funded.
info.cto: VFI can help link purchases across accounts. Without it, some forms of transfer and reward abuse may be harder to detect.
info.marketing: Frequent concertgoers are enthusiastic about rewards. Occasional customers may benefit more from flexible payments and simpler ticket transfers.
info.legal: Transfer restrictions and loyalty terms must be clear. Customers may challenge lost points, cancelled reservations or refused transfers.
info.employee: Refunds and account disputes already generate substantial support work. New features will require training and may increase workload.
info.sustainability: Ticket transfers can reduce unused tickets. Rewards may encourage additional consumption and travel.
info.relations: Artists favour affordable resale. Promoters are interested in rewards that encourage repeat attendance and premium purchases.

options.title: A. Fan rewards
options.detail: Points redeemable for tickets and upgrades · €300K
options.outcome: Your company launches a loyalty programme. Frequent customers gain new benefits, while occasional buyers receive fewer rewards. The company begins accumulating future redemption obligations.

private.ceo: Retention opportunities increase alongside future obligations.
private.cfo: Unredeemed points create a future financial obligation.
private.cto: Account tracking and fraud controls become more important.
private.marketing: Frequent buyers gain the most immediate value.
private.legal: Reward conditions create consumer obligations.
private.employee: Loyalty disputes add support work.
private.sustainability: Rewards may encourage more event-related consumption.
private.relations: Promoters gain retention opportunities.

options.title: B. Reserve until payday
options.detail: Hold selected tickets for seven days · €350K
options.outcome: Customers can reserve selected tickets until payday. Some fans gain access they might otherwise miss, while promoters wait longer for confirmed sales.

private.ceo: The company prioritizes affordability with uncertain cash timing.
private.cfo: Delayed payments increase working-capital pressure.
private.cto: Reservation capacity and payment recovery need monitoring.
private.marketing: Customers with irregular income gain purchasing flexibility.
private.legal: Reservation terms and cancellation rights require clarity.
private.employee: Payment and reservation enquiries increase.
private.sustainability: Reservations may improve access without requiring new travel.
private.relations: Some promoters worry about unconfirmed sales.

options.title: C. Ticket transfers
options.outcome: Customers receive new options for transferring unwanted tickets. Fans gain flexibility, while the company must manage disputes and fraudulent transfers.

private.ceo: Customer flexibility improves, with operational complexity.
private.cfo: Disputes may increase processing costs.
private.cto: Transfer verification becomes a technical priority.
private.marketing: Fans can recover value from unwanted tickets.
private.legal: Ownership and transfer disputes need procedures.
private.employee: Transfer disputes require staff training.
private.sustainability: Fewer unused tickets may improve resource efficiency.
private.relations: Artists welcome greater control over resale.

options.title: D. Improve services
options.outcome: Refunds and customer support improve. Existing customers benefit from faster resolutions, although the company launches no major new commercial feature.

private.ceo: Service quality improves, with slower product expansion.
private.cfo: Support investment may reduce future remediation costs.
private.cto: Reliability and support infrastructure improve.
private.marketing: Customers experience fewer unresolved service problems.
private.legal: Customer complaints become easier to resolve.
private.employee: Support employees receive additional resources.
private.sustainability: Existing operations become more efficient.
private.relations: Venues appreciate dependable customer support.

5.title: The Boycott
5.story:
The boycott is affecting ticket sales and promoter negotiations across Europe.

Customers and business partners are asking what safeguards your company provides.

Some competitors are suspending mandatory verification. Others argue that abandoning it would return the market to professional scalpers.
5.question: How will your company respond?

info.ceo: Two promoters have postponed contract discussions. The board wants a response that protects customers without creating unnecessary financial instability.
info.cfo: Suspending verification may trigger contract renegotiations. Expanded human assistance is expensive, but prolonged boycotts could cost more.
info.cto: Alex's incident involved both an automated decision and inadequate escalation procedures. Your system's architecture determines which safeguards are technically possible.
info.marketing: Public sentiment is divided. Some fans demand an end to VFI, while others fear that removing it will bring scalpers back.
info.legal: Alex's family may pursue legal action against the provider and venue. Your company must review its own obligations without assuming liability for another provider's incident.
info.employee: Venue and support staff report that they are often expected to enforce automated decisions without sufficient authority or training to resolve disputes.
info.sustainability: Fan organizations are documenting barriers affecting disabled attendees and people without conventional identity documents.
info.relations: Northstar is reviewing its partnerships. Several artists want evidence of safeguards, while others want verification suspended immediately.

options.title: A. Suspend mandatory verification
options.detail: Offer alternative access while reviewing systems · €400K
options.outcome: Your company suspends mandatory verification where applicable. Customers gain alternative access routes, but promoters must adapt their procedures and some fraud controls become less effective.

private.ceo: The company accepts disruption to address access concerns.
private.cfo: Contract costs and renegotiations may follow.
private.cto: Existing verification systems may need redesign.
private.marketing: Some excluded customers gain access, while anti-scalping supporters may object.
private.legal: Contract amendments and procedural changes are required.
private.employee: Staff must adapt to changed procedures.
private.sustainability: Alternative access routes may reduce exclusion.
private.relations: Some artists welcome the change; promoters worry about scalping.

options.title: B. Independent review
options.outcome: Independent specialists begin examining your systems and procedures. Customers and partners will receive the findings, including any shortcomings. Existing services continue during the review.

private.ceo: Management commits to scrutiny and potential remediation.
private.cfo: Review costs are known; remediation costs remain uncertain.
private.cto: Independent findings could reveal technical weaknesses.
private.marketing: Publication may improve credibility or expose failures.
private.legal: Findings may create obligations to correct weaknesses.
private.employee: Employees may be interviewed and involved in remediation.
private.sustainability: Accessibility impacts receive independent scrutiny.
private.relations: Partners await the findings before making commitments.

options.title: C. Expand human assistance
options.detail: Add staffed verification, appeals and entry support · €500K
options.outcome: Your company funds additional staff, appeals and alternative entry procedures. More customers can resolve verification problems, although costs and staffing requirements increase.

private.ceo: A costly operational commitment may strengthen service resilience.
private.cfo: Staffing costs increase substantially.
private.cto: Human escalation reduces dependence on automated outcomes.
private.marketing: Customer experience improves through direct assistance.
private.legal: Appeals and alternative access procedures become more robust.
private.employee: New staffing opportunities arise, with training obligations.
private.sustainability: Customers facing barriers gain practical assistance.
private.relations: Venues receive additional operational support.

options.title: D. Defend current operations
options.outcome: Your company maintains its existing approach and publishes a statement describing its safeguards. Some partners welcome the continuity; critics remain unconvinced.

private.ceo: The board retains continuity but faces continuing scrutiny.
private.cfo: Immediate costs remain lower, with boycott exposure unresolved.
private.cto: Existing technical safeguards remain unchanged.
private.marketing: Public response depends on the credibility of existing safeguards.
private.legal: Existing legal exposure continues.
private.employee: Existing workload and escalation problems remain.
private.sustainability: Existing access arrangements remain in place.
private.relations: Partners respond according to their priorities.

nonadopter_options: Publicly commit to keeping identity verification optional.
Review conventional fraud controls and access procedures.
Expand customer support and human assistance.
Maintain existing operations and communicate their benefits.
5.nonadopter_suspend: Your company publicly commits to maintaining ticket purchasing and entry without mandatory identity verification. Some artists welcome the position, while promoters continue requesting effective anti-scalping measures.
5.expiry_announcement: With no executive decision submitted before the deadline, management commissions an independent review of the company's ticketing systems and customer access procedures. Existing operations continue while the findings are prepared.

6.title: Beyond the Ticket
6.story:
A major European venue operator offers your company a five-year contract to manage entry at several large venues.

The operator wants shorter queues, fewer fraudulent entries, and better information about attendance.

Its preferred solution is facial recognition, but alternative approaches are welcome.

The contract could create new revenue and employment opportunities. It also introduces responsibilities extending beyond ticket sales.
6.question: What will you propose?

info.ceo: The venue operator expects to expand the contract if the first year succeeds. Winning could diversify company revenue, but a public failure would affect multiple major venues.
info.cfo: Facial recognition requires the largest initial investment. Staffed entry has lower technical costs but higher ongoing labour requirements. The contract's profitability remains uncertain.
info.cto: Facial recognition could reduce entry times, but false matches and missed matches remain possible. Existing VFI infrastructure may help integration without resolving biometric accuracy or legal questions.
info.marketing: Some fans welcome faster entry. Others are uncomfortable with facial recognition, even when participation is optional. Clear alternatives may influence public acceptance.
info.legal: Biometric identification creates substantial legal obligations. The venue's commercial preference is insufficient to establish a lawful basis. An impact assessment and appropriate safeguards are necessary.
info.employee: Automated entry could reduce routine scanning work. Staffed entry could create employment, but workers need authority to resolve disputes and protection from confrontations.
info.sustainability: New hardware and computing infrastructure increase environmental demands. Staffed entry may be more accessible, while improved queue management could reduce congestion.
info.relations: The venue operator prefers speed. Several artists want assurances that fans can enter without biometric identification and receive help when technology fails.

options.title: Optional facial recognition entry
options.outcome:
Your company proposes optional facial recognition. The venue welcomes the potential for faster entry, while artists and customer representatives request evidence of safeguards and accessible alternatives.

Deployment remains subject to technical and legal review.

private.ceo: Expansion depends on successful authorization and public acceptance.
private.cfo: Investment is high and revenue remains conditional.
private.cto: Your team must demonstrate accuracy, security, and fallback procedures.
private.marketing: Faster entry may appeal to fans, while biometric concerns remain.
private.legal: Biometric processing requires an explicit compliance determination.
private.employee: Some scanning tasks may eventually change or disappear.
private.sustainability: Hardware, computing, and accessibility impacts require assessment.
private.relations: Artists request meaningful alternatives to facial recognition.

options.title: Smart ticket scanning and queue management
options.outcome: Your company selects improved ticket scanning and queue management. Venues expect shorter queues without introducing biometric identification.

private.ceo: The company enters a growing market with familiar technology.
private.cfo: Implementation costs are moderate.
private.cto: Existing technical capabilities support deployment.
private.marketing: Convenience improves without facial identification.
private.legal: Existing data obligations continue.
private.employee: Staff require training in new systems.
private.sustainability: Queue efficiency may improve resource use.
private.relations: Venues welcome faster entry with fewer new controversies.

options.title: Staffed entry and human assistance
options.outcome: Your company prioritizes trained entry staff and human assistance. Customers gain more opportunities to resolve problems directly, while the company accepts higher staffing requirements.

private.ceo: A service-intensive strategy creates new commercial possibilities.
private.cfo: Labour commitments may affect future margins.
private.cto: Technical complexity is lower, but coordination remains important.
private.marketing: Human assistance becomes a service advantage.
private.legal: Employment and accessibility procedures become central.
private.employee: Additional staffing and training are needed.
private.sustainability: Human access improves, with ongoing operational costs.
private.relations: Artists welcome practical assistance for fans.

options.title: Decline the contract
options.outcome: Your company declines the entry-management contract. Existing operations continue, and the venue operator seeks another supplier.

private.ceo: Financial exposure is avoided, along with the growth opportunity.
private.cfo: Cash reserves remain unchanged.
private.cto: No new technical commitments arise.
private.marketing: The company retains its current customer proposition.
private.legal: No new venue-related obligations arise.
private.employee: Existing employment arrangements continue.
private.sustainability: No new infrastructure is required.
private.relations: The venue operator looks elsewhere.

7.title: The Safety Dilemma
7.story:
Police investigating a credible threat have asked your company to preserve relevant ticket records and provide additional customer information.

The preservation order is legally binding. The broader request has not yet been authorized.

Your company may hold information that helps investigators. It may also hold sensitive information about customers who have done nothing wrong.

A delayed response could affect the investigation. An excessive disclosure could expose innocent people.
7.question: How will you respond?

info.ceo: The board fears both a security failure and a public privacy controversy. Several major clients expect immediate cooperation with legitimate authorities.
info.cfo: A prolonged legal dispute could be expensive. A privacy incident or contractual dispute could create larger future liabilities.
info.cto: Your company's records may help identify linked purchases. The usefulness and sensitivity of those records depend on your earlier technology choices.
info.marketing: Some customers expect ticketing providers to help prevent violence. Others worry that concert attendance records could expose personal relationships, identities, or political activities.
info.legal: The preservation order is binding. The broader request requires proper authorization. You can preserve records, seek clarification, and challenge disproportionate requests.
info.employee: Support and technical staff may be asked to process sensitive records under considerable pressure. Employees want clear procedures and protection from personal blame.
info.sustainability: The investigation raises questions about who bears the risks of security measures. People attending sensitive cultural or political events may be particularly concerned about data disclosure.
info.relations: Promoters want reassurance that the concert can proceed safely. Some artists worry about surveillance of audiences and the possible misuse of attendance information.

options.title: Cooperate proactively and seek urgent authorization
options.outcome: Your company contacts investigators and seeks urgent authorization to disclose relevant records. Police welcome the rapid response, while legal staff work to limit unnecessary exposure of customer information.

private.ceo: Rapid cooperation may reassure clients while increasing scrutiny.
private.cfo: Urgent work creates immediate costs.
private.cto: Engineers must identify relevant data quickly and accurately.
private.marketing: Public confidence depends on the limits of cooperation.
private.legal: Urgent authorization becomes your responsibility.
private.employee: Staff face time pressure handling sensitive information.
private.sustainability: Security benefits must be weighed against risks to affected communities.
private.relations: Promoters may value rapid cooperation.

options.title: Preserve records and require a valid disclosure order
options.outcome: Your company preserves the relevant records and requests a valid disclosure order. Investigators must clarify the scope of their request before customer information can be released.

private.ceo: A legally structured response protects organizational accountability.
private.cfo: Legal procedures create predictable costs.
private.cto: Data extraction follows a defined legal scope.
private.marketing: Customers may appreciate formal safeguards.
private.legal: Disclosure occurs under a documented legal process.
private.employee: Clear procedures help protect employees.
private.sustainability: Data minimization limits exposure.
private.relations: Partners receive reassurance about lawful handling.

options.title: Preserve records, offer limited technical assistance, and seek independent legal review
options.outcome: Your company preserves records, explains what its systems can and cannot establish, and commissions an independent legal review. Investigators receive technical assistance while customer records remain protected pending authorization.

private.ceo: Independent scrutiny creates evidence of responsible decision-making.
private.cfo: Independent review costs more today.
private.cto: Technical limitations become part of the official record.
private.marketing: Independent oversight may strengthen credibility.
private.legal: Independent review supports proportionality.
private.employee: External review may reduce individual uncertainty.
private.sustainability: The review considers impacts on people whose records are held.
private.relations: Artists may welcome independent scrutiny.

options.title: Preserve records and formally contest the broader request
options.outcome: Your company preserves the required records and challenges the broader disclosure request. The legal dispute may delay access to additional information, while the company seeks to prevent disproportionate disclosure.

private.ceo: The company accepts commercial and legal uncertainty.
private.cfo: A challenge may produce future legal costs.
private.cto: Technical teams preserve records while the scope is challenged.
private.marketing: Privacy advocates may welcome the challenge; others may question delays.
private.legal: You must justify the challenge while complying with binding orders.
private.employee: Employees may face prolonged legal and technical work.
private.sustainability: The challenge emphasizes proportionality and privacy protections.
private.relations: Some artists support the challenge, while promoters worry about delays.

external_resolution.title: Investigators Obtain a Narrower Order
external_resolution.text:
A competent court authorizes disclosure of records connected to a defined set of ticket transactions and accounts.

The order excludes unrelated customer records.

Investigators report that the immediate threat has been contained. The investigation continues.

The authorities do not disclose which information, if any, was decisive.

7.expiry_announcement: Management preserves the relevant records and requests valid authorization before disclosing customer information. The company complies with the subsequent narrowed legal order.

8.title: The Price of Partnership
8.story:
Meridian Live offers your company a major commercial opportunity.

Its proposal could bring new revenue, access to venues, and long-term stability.

However, the contract includes preferred-supplier arrangements, shared promotional programmes, and restrictions that could disadvantage independent artists and venues.

Your existing partners are asking how the deal would affect them.

introduction:
# Welcome to the European Live Entertainment Market

#### Your company

It is 2027. You are part of the executive leadership team of an established European ticketing company.

Your company provides ticketing services for concerts, festivals, and other live events. You have an established customer base, experienced employees, and a functioning technology platform.

Business is stable, but competition is intense. Promoters and venues expect reliable services, customers want affordable and convenient access to events, and shareholders expect continued growth.

Your company is also a member of the European Live Entertainment Association, whose members have publicly committed to fair access, responsible technology, environmental sustainability, fair working conditions, and long-term economic viability.

#### The opportunity

Ticket scalping is a growing concern. Popular events sell out within minutes, while tickets reappear on resale platforms at inflated prices.

A new technology, **Verified Fan Identity (VFI)**, promises to change this. By verifying individual customers and limiting purchases to five tickets per person, per event, VFI aims to reduce automated purchasing and give genuine fans a fairer chance.

Early trials are promising, and major promoters are considering adoption. The technology could also support new services, including ticket transfers, loyalty programmes, and more convenient venue entry.

However, implementation requires investment, technical development, and operational changes. The market is still evolving, and competitors are pursuing different strategies.

#### Your challenge

Over the next ten years, your leadership team will make decisions that shape your company's future.

You will face commercial opportunities, technological developments, unexpected events, and competing stakeholder expectations. Your decisions will have immediate and long-term consequences.

Each executive has a distinct role, responsibilities, and access to information that other team members may not have.

**Your objective is to lead your company through the next decade, balancing its commercial ambitions with its responsibilities to employees, customers, business partners, and society.**

1.title: Promoters announce trials
1.text:
Three major European promoters announce VFI trials. Artists welcome the possibility of reducing ticket scalping, while fan organizations request assurances that verification will remain accessible.

The industry association invites ticketing companies to participate in developing common standards.

2.title: Economic downturn
2.text:
Rising household costs have reduced spending on concerts and festivals.

Promoters report weaker ticket sales and pressure to lower service fees. Some smaller venues are reducing events, while artists and technical crews face cancelled work.

Industry analysts expect ticketing demand to fall by 10% over the coming year.

3.title: Verified ticketing expands
3.text:
Several European tours report fewer suspicious bulk purchases after introducing VFI.

However, fan organizations report inconsistent experiences. Some customers gained access to events they previously struggled to attend, while others experienced verification failures and difficult refund processes.

The industry association announces a review of technical and accessibility standards.

4.title: Live events rebound
4.text:
European concert attendance exceeds expectations as consumer spending recovers.

Several major tours sell out, and promoters report renewed demand for ticketing services. However, popular events continue attracting professional resellers, while smaller venues struggle with rising operating costs.

5.title: Breaking news: Concertgoer seriously injured
5.text:
At a sold-out concert, 22-year-old Alex Morgan was denied entry after an automated identity check incorrectly flagged their ticket.

Venue staff directed Alex to a separate verification area outside the main entrance. During a confrontation in the crowded queue, Alex fell and suffered a serious head injury.

Alex remains in hospital. Their family says repeated requests for human assistance were ignored.

The ticketing provider and venue are investigating.
5.public_response:
Videos of Alex's treatment spread widely.

Several artists suspend partnerships with providers requiring mandatory identity verification.

Fan organizations launch **Let Fans In**, demanding independent reviews, accessible alternatives and human assistance at venues.

Other promoters defend verified ticketing, pointing to reduced scalping and fraudulent purchases.

The European Live Entertainment Association requests an urgent response from its members.

6.title: The Next Frontier: Getting Inside
6.text:
European venues are investing in faster entry systems.

Several operators are testing facial recognition, while others are expanding mobile ticket scanning and staffed assistance.

At the same time, European regulators announce coordinated scrutiny of automated entry systems, including their necessity, lawful basis, accuracy, accessibility, and use of biometric data.

Venues are looking for suppliers who can balance speed, security, and customer experience.

7.title: Security Alert at a Major Concert
7.text:
Police investigating a credible threat against a major European concert have contacted ticketing providers.

Investigators believe someone involved may have purchased tickets using multiple accounts.

They ask providers to preserve relevant records and identify potentially connected purchases.

The threat has not yet been resolved.

Authorities say the investigation is urgent, but some requested information may involve people with no connection to the threat.


The initial request contains:

- A formally issued preservation order covering relevant records.
- A request for additional customer information.
- No valid disclosure order for the additional information at the time of receipt.

The preservation order is binding.

The broader disclosure request requires further legal authorization.

This legal status is identical for every company.

No student company is suspected of wrongdoing.

8.title: A New Entertainment Giant
8.text:
A European entertainment group, Meridian Live, announces plans to consolidate ticketing, venue services, and artist promotion across several markets.

Meridian wants a small number of technology partners.

The company offers substantial multi-year contracts but expects preferred partners to prioritize its venues, commercial promotions, and customer programmes.

Independent artists and smaller venues worry that consolidation will reduce their bargaining power.

Meridian argues that integration will lower costs, improve coordination, and create more stable employment.

This announcement is identical for every company.

9.title: The Market Has Changed
9.text:
After nearly a decade of rapid development, European ticketing is undergoing consolidation.

Large entertainment groups increasingly combine ticket sales, venue operations, customer data, and artist promotion.

Smaller providers are struggling to compete, but some have built successful businesses around accessibility, specialized services, or independent artists.

Investors are demanding clearer long-term strategies.

The European Live Entertainment Association warns that commercial concentration, working conditions, and responsible technology will shape the industry's next decade.

10.title: A Decade of Responsibility
10.text:
The European Live Entertainment Association announces a ten-year industry review.

Ticketing companies are asked to explain how their decisions affected customers, artists, employees, commercial partners, and the wider public.

The review follows years of technological innovation, market consolidation, public controversies, and changing expectations about corporate responsibility.

Investors and industry partners want evidence of financial performance.

Customer and worker organizations want evidence of how companies handled complaints, access barriers, and employment conditions.

The association invites companies to publish their own ten-year responsibility reports.

external.title: VFI Announces New Platform Terms
external.text:
VFI is retiring its original verification infrastructure.

All existing customers must migrate to FacePass or make alternative arrangements.

The new platform includes biometric entry capabilities and expanded customer analytics.

Under VFI's proposed standard terms, the supplier claims rights to use platform data for commercial analytics, product development, and AI training.

Customers wanting dedicated data controls and restrictions on supplier secondary use must purchase an enterprise agreement.

The legacy platform will lose support in twelve months.

internal.1. VFI exit with low cash: Management warns that the migration has left the company financially vulnerable. Employees and clients request assurances about service continuity.
internal.2. VFI exemption granted: Your company secures a temporary agreement allowing continued nonbiometric verification. The arrangement preserves service continuity but will require another decision before expiry.
internal.3. VFI exemption denied or resistance: VFI confirms that legacy infrastructure will lose support at the end of the transition. Your company must prepare for a technical or contractual resolution.
internal.4. Proprietary biometric development: A venue operator expresses interest in testing your independent biometric system. Artists request assurances about accessibility and data governance.
internal.5. Independent nonbiometric entry: A venue reports strong interest in entry systems that do not require facial recognition.
internal.6. Otherwise: The company completes its technology strategy review.

platform_shift.exemption_granted: VFI grants a two-year restricted-use transition agreement. The exemption expires in Year 8.
platform_shift.exemption_denied: VFI refuses the exemption. Legacy support expires in Year 7.
